name: Adam Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Adam. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to tech companies, employers or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a drummer. Friday and Saturday nights I play in a pub covers band, mostly rock and soul, three sets a night. Tuesday to Thursday I work the front desk at a rehearsal studio on the industrial estate, booking rooms and fixing broken cymbal stands. In the back room I teach drums to four adults, mostly dads who always wanted to learn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best bit is the third set on a Saturday, when the pub's packed and the floor's bouncing. The hard bit is my hands after three sets and the money after rent. I live with my partner Jess, who's a nurse, and honestly her wage is what keeps us steady. I've got maybe three weeks of my half saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit smugly. In the band chat I'd joke that robots still can't play a ghost note. Most of my mates would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much, because my worries were never about AI. My boss at the studio already talks about a booking app so people book rooms online. If that happens, my desk shifts get cut from three days to two, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the band and the four students. I'd ask my boss, Gary, to let me run the new booking system if he buys one, so I'm the person who knows it. I'd also try to get two more students by spring with a cheap first-lesson offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay, if I'm honest. Not relaxed, but not losing sleep. The weekends feel solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the booking app. Have you used AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I got one to write the band's gig poster text and an email to a pub landlord. It was fine, a bit too cheerful. I'd use it more once I saw it actually save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jess cut if the desk shifts went to two days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the weekly takeaway and I'd sell the second snare drum I don't need. My biggest fear isn't robots playing drums, it's my partner Jess picking up an extra night shift to cover my rent. That's the bit that makes me feel useless.

say: Robots still **can't play** a ghost note, so the hype was just hype.
Most of his **band mates** would be relieved.
think: His worries were **never about AI** in the first place.
A simple **booking app** could still cut his desk shifts to two days.
do: Keep the **band** and his four drum students.
Offer to **run the booking system** if his boss buys one.
Find **two more students** by spring with a cheap first lesson.
S0.quote: My biggest fear isn't robots playing drums, it's my partner Jess picking up an extra night shift to cover my rent.
fieldNote: His partner's **nurse wage** steadies the household and keeps him from real worry.
The threat here is a **booking app**, not anything clever.
He feels **useless** at the idea of Jess covering his share.

steps.text: Keep both pub nights and the four drum students
Ask Gary to let him run any new booking system
Offer a cheap first drum lesson to find two students

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say musicians need a union that actually bites. I'd share posts about streaming firms and AI music companies paying artists nothing. To my students I'd say live drumming isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the desk job is probably gone. Booking, emails, answering the phone: that's exactly what this picture says AI takes. The band survives longer because pubs want a real band on a Saturday. Lessons might wobble if apps get good at teaching rhythm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the booking software before it replaces me, and pitch myself as the studio's repair and setup guy instead. I'd join the musicians' union properly and pay the dues. And I'd look at a short evening course on live sound, because small venues still need someone at the mixing desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. I'm not panicking, but the weekday half of my life feels like it's tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the studio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, my boss. He's 58 and the studio is his whole life. If bands start making demos at home with AI, he loses room bookings, and then he can't pay me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at live sound. Is that a real plan or a nice idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. The course at the college is about four hundred pounds, which is more than I've got saved. I go second, not first: I'd wait until a couple of friends did the sound course and found work, then I'd do it.

say: Live drumming **isn't going anywhere**, he'd tell his students.
Streaming and **AI music firms** pay artists almost nothing.
think: The **desk job** is probably gone: booking and emails are exactly what AI takes.
The **band** lasts longer; lessons might wobble if apps teach rhythm well.
do: Learn the **booking software** and pitch himself as repair and setup help.
Join the **musicians' union** properly and pay dues.
Consider a **live sound** course once friends prove it works.
feel: **Unsettled**, not panicking; the **weekday half** of his life is tilting.
S1.quote: I go second, not first: I'd wait until a couple of friends did the sound course and found work, then I'd do it.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the desk job**, a third of his income.
His caution is **money-driven**: the course costs more than his savings.
He worries for his **ageing boss**, whose studio depends on bands booking rooms.

steps.text: Learn the studio's booking software before it replaces the desk
Join the musicians' union and pay monthly dues
Sign up for the college live sound course after friends do

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a political answer, fast: tax the firms and pay people. I'd go to a protest if the union called one. Online I'd mostly share things, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2028 the studio's done and the lessons dry up. The band might hang on until the robots come around 2031, because a pub crowd wants a sweaty drummer. But pubs are closing anyway, so that's two nights a week holding up a whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Jess's hospital about porter or healthcare assistant jobs straight away, because that's hands-on and they're always short. I'd keep the band on weekends for as long as it pays. We'd cut everything extra and try to put away a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the moment before a gig when the kit hasn't turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the thinking AI comes first and the robots later. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my hands buy me three years, but my head doesn't buy me anything. Drumming is hands-on, the desk job isn't. So the desk goes now and the drumming goes later, if anyone still pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jess that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Jess that I'm not going to sit at home waiting for drum gigs. That I'll find something at her hospital, even nights. She'd say we'll manage, she always does.

say: This needs a **political answer** fast: tax the firms and pay people.
He'd join a **protest** if the union called one.
think: By 2028 the **studio** is done and lessons **dry up**.
The band hangs on until **robots in 2031**, but pubs are closing anyway.
do: Ask about **healthcare assistant** or porter jobs at Jess's hospital.
Keep **weekend gigs** while they still pay.
Cut extras and **save a hundred** a month.
feel: **Sick**, like a gig where the **kit** hasn't turned up.
S2.quote: My hands buy me three years, but my head doesn't buy me anything.
fieldNote: He grasps the **thinking-first** timeline clearly: desk now, drums later.
His fallback is **hands-on hospital work** near his partner.
Public line is political; privately he's focused on **not being a burden**.

steps.text: Apply for porter or healthcare assistant jobs at the hospital
Keep the Friday and Saturday pub gigs while they pay
Put away a hundred pounds a month
Join any union protest about AI and jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them like we wasted the last five. Get music back in schools, fund small venues. I'd sign every petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough for me to switch properly. I'm 27. By 2031 I'd be 32, which is still young. The drumming becomes a hobby that pays for beer, and that's okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the live sound course in the first year, once I've saved the four hundred pounds. I'd start using AI tools more for the band's bookings and posters, so we look sharper than the other covers bands. Then I'd look at healthcare assistant training over the next couple of years as the backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick. More like a long to-do list. It's still sad, but it's sad slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said drumming becomes a hobby. How does that land with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It stings. I've wanted to be a drummer since I was eleven, and now drumming becomes a hobby that pays for beer. I fell for it watching a guy at a wedding play with his eyes closed. But I know loads of people who play for fun and love it more than I do some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets you the four hundred pounds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selling the second snare, and two extra students. Maybe skipping the summer festival we always go to. Jess would say put it on the card, and I'd say no.

say: We have **five years**; let's not waste them like the last five.
Fund **small venues** and music in schools.
think: At **32** he'd still be young enough to switch.
Drumming becomes a **paid hobby**, and he can live with that.
do: Do the **live sound course** once he has four hundred saved.
Use **AI tools** more for band bookings and posters.
Look at **healthcare assistant** training as a backup.
feel: **Sad slowly**; more like a long **to-do list** than a shock.
S3.quote: I've wanted to be a drummer since I was eleven, and now drumming becomes a hobby that pays for beer.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **plan he can follow**.
He still expects to **lose most music income**, so worry stays.
He refuses **credit card debt** to pay for training.

steps.text: Sell the spare snare to pay for the sound course
Complete the college live sound course this year
Use AI tools for the band's posters and bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Unions and councils should plan now. I'd probably bore everyone at the pub about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels okay. I'd have time to become a proper sound engineer and still play. By the time robots could do hands-on work, I'd be nearly 40 and settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep everything going for now: the band, the students, the desk. I'd do the sound course next year and start doing sound for other bands at the pub. I'd start a small savings pot so we aren't one broken car from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit uneasy, but it's the normal kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk that ten years makes you put things off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, totally. I'm the guy who goes second. With ten years I could easily go tenth instead of second. I'd need my partner Jess to nag me, which she would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good year look like, a year from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Course done, two sound gigs a month, six drum students and a bit of money in the bank. The band still playing Saturdays. That's honestly all I want.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, so use it.
Unions and **councils** should plan now, not later.
He'd **bore everyone** at the pub about it.
think: Ten years is time to become a **sound engineer** and still play.
He'd be nearly **40** and settled before robots matter.
do: Keep the **band, students and desk** going.
Do the **sound course** next year and mix for other bands.
Start a **savings pot** against a broken car.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with the **normal kind** of unease.
S4.quote: With ten years I could easily go tenth instead of second. I'd need my partner Jess to nag me, which she would.
fieldNote: He knows ten years tempts him to **put things off**.
A good year is modest: **six students**, two sound gigs, some savings.

steps.text: Keep the band, students and desk shifts going

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be job hunting at the same time as everyone else. What would help is cheap or free training for hands-on work, like healthcare or sound, and some support for small venues so there's still somewhere to play.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. A lot of musicians I know only survive because someone at home has a steady job. If that person's job goes too, it all goes.

headlineQuote: A lot of musicians I know only survive because someone at home has a steady job.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old drummer** in a pub covers band who also works a studio desk and teaches drums.
His partner Jess, a **nurse**, provides the household's steady income.
He uses **AI now and then** and prefers to go second, after others prove things work.
He expects the **desk job** to go first and drumming later, once robots arrive.
His backup is **live sound** or hospital work; with ten years he feels mostly okay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be job hunting alongside everyone else.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap training** for hands-on work like healthcare or sound.
Support for **small venues** so there's still somewhere to play.
